title: Definite Integrals & The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
outcomes: Evaluate definite integrals of linear functions using antiderivatives and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
Compute exact rational definite integrals of quadratic polynomials over Q using the reverse power rule int x^2 dx = x^3 / 3.
Apply the Net Change Theorem s(t) = s(0) + int_0^t v(tau) dtau to recover exact position from velocity and initial value.

sections.intuition: How does signed area under a rate-of-change curve y = f(x) connect to derivatives? If A(x) = ∫₀^x f(t) dt tracks the accumulated area up to x, advancing x by a tiny width Δx adds a thin strip of area approximately f(x)·Δx, so A'(x) = f(x). Therefore, accumulation and differentiation are inverse operations! To compute the exact definite integral ∫_a^b f(x) dx, we find any antiderivative F(x) satisfying F'(x) = f(x) and evaluate the net change F(b) - F(a).
sections.formal_definition:
1. Reverse Power Rule for Antiderivatives: For integer n ≥ 0, an antiderivative of x^n is x^(n+1)/(n + 1) because d/dx[x^(n+1)/(n + 1)] = x^n.
2. Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Evaluation Theorem): If f is continuous on [a, b] and F'(x) = f(x), then
∫_a^b f(x) dx = [F(x)]_a^b = F(b) - F(a).
3. Net Change Theorem: Given velocity v(t) = s'(t) and initial position s(0),
s(t) = s(0) + ∫₀^t v(τ) dτ.
sections.worked_example:
Evaluate ∫₀² (4x² + 3) dx over ℚ.
1. Find an antiderivative using the reverse power rule: F(x) = (4/3)x³ + 3x.
2. Evaluate at the upper limit x = 2: F(2) = (4/3)(2³) + 3(2) = 32/3 + 6 = 32/3 + 18/3 = 50/3.
3. Evaluate at the lower limit x = 0: F(0) = 0.
4. Subtract: F(2) - F(0) = 50/3.
common_misconceptions: Forgetting to divide by the new exponent (n + 1) when antidifferentiating x^n (e.g., antidifferentiating ax² as ax³ instead of (a/3)x³).
Treating a constant term c as c instead of c·x in the antiderivative.
Reporting only the net displacement ∫₀^t v(τ) dτ without adding the initial value s(0).
